result: HA and NA are asymmetrically distributed on the surface of filamentous IAV particles, with approximately one-third of particles showing at least 5-fold enrichment of NA at one pole. NA tends to colocalize with the viral genome (NP) at one pole, with ~2-fold enrichment relative to HA. This distribution is stable over tens of minutes and is observed at both diffraction-limited and super-resolution scales.
evaluation: Claims C3, C13-C19 provide converging evidence from multiple imaging modalities (fluorescence microscopy, STORM) with large sample sizes (>20,000 particles for C13, 4,805 for C14) showing consistent asymmetric distribution of HA and NA. The photobleaching experiments (C16) demonstrate stability, and quantitative metrics are provided with appropriate statistical measures.

result: Viruses that escaped cell surfaces under neuraminidase inhibitor (NAI) challenge showed significantly higher HA-NA polarity (0.155) compared to viruses released without NAI challenge (0.123 before and 0.100 after exogenous sialidase treatment), suggesting that polarized NA distribution may enhance navigation through sialic acid-rich environments.
evaluation: Claim C20 provides quantitative data with confidence intervals from NAI challenge experiments (Figure 1G). The functional interpretation in C21 is appropriately cautious ('may be more effective') and is supported by the experimental design comparing viruses under different release conditions. The result demonstrates a correlation between NA polarity and ability to escape under challenging conditions.

result: Filamentous viruses with polarized NA distributions exhibit persistent directional mobility away from their NA-rich pole on sialic acid-coated surfaces. This directional mobility can persist for several microns and is accompanied by receptor destruction. Mobile viruses (~68% of the population) have significantly more polarized HA-NA distributions than non-mobile viruses.
evaluation: Claims C24-C28 are supported by direct experimental observations using time-lapse microscopy (Figure 2B, Video 1), ECL labeling showing receptor cleavage trails (C25), trajectory analysis (C26), and quantitative comparison of mobile vs. non-mobile populations (C28, Figure 2E). The large sample size (n=347 mobile viruses) and statistical testing strengthen the conclusions.

result: Deletion of the NA cytoplasmic tail (NAΔCT) reduces NA packaging into virions, renders NA clusters mobile on the viral surface, significantly decreases NA polarity on the viral surface, and eliminates persistent directional motion, demonstrating that the cytoplasmic tail is necessary for both NA localization and directional mobility.
evaluation: Claims C29-C35 describe a well-designed genetic perturbation experiment with multiple complementary measurements (imaging, STORM, photobleaching, motility assays). The loss of directional motion in NAΔCT viruses (C35) directly supports the causal role of NA spatial organization. Data is shown in multiple supplementary figures with appropriate quantification.

result: Wildtype viruses show ~5-fold enhancement in diffusion coefficient due to directional correlations, while NAΔCT viruses show only ~1.5-fold enhancement. Wildtype viruses step toward the HA-rich pole approximately twice as frequently as the opposite direction, while NAΔCT viruses show no directional preference.
evaluation: Claims C37-C40 provide quantitative comparisons between wildtype and NAΔCT viruses using mean squared displacement analysis (Figure 3B) and stepping angle analysis (Figure 3C). The measurements are based on trajectory data from multiple biological replicates and provide clear evidence for the functional importance of NA polarization in directional mobility.

result: NAΔCT viruses leave significantly larger trails of cleaved receptors than wildtype viruses despite having lower NA content, demonstrating that spatial organization and mobility of NA on the viral surface determine where and when substrate cleavage occurs.
evaluation: Claims C41-C42 are supported by ECL trail analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). The counterintuitive finding that viruses with less NA create larger trails is well-documented and supports the mechanistic interpretation that NA localization, not just abundance, controls cleavage patterns. This is a key result linking protein organization to enzymatic function.

result: Computational modeling shows that virus diffusion is constrained by multiple HA-sialic acid attachments, and NA at the interface between HA-rich and NA-rich regions creates a gradient in sialic acid density along the virus length. This gradient drives persistent directional motion, which is lost when NA distribution becomes symmetric or when NA is allowed to freely diffuse.
evaluation: Claims C43-C48 describe computational simulations that recapitulate experimental observations and provide mechanistic insight. The simulations (Figure 3—figure supplement 5) show how NA polarization creates asymmetric sialic acid distributions that bias virus motion. The agreement between simulations and experiments (C48) strengthens both sets of results.

result: Computational simulations predict that sialic acid diffusion can either enhance or suppress directional motion depending on the diffusion coefficient. Polarized IAV bound to slowly-diffusing receptors (DSA <0.01 µm²/s) will exhibit enhanced mobility, while faster diffusion (DSA >0.01 µm²/s) suppresses persistent motion. Increasing virus length increases directional persistence but reduces overall mobility.
evaluation: Claims C49-C52 extend the computational model to explore parameter space beyond experimental conditions. The predictions are clearly stated and supported by simulation data (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 6). However, these remain predictions that would benefit from experimental validation, particularly for the effects of receptor mobility.

result: In three-dimensional mucus gels produced by Calu-3 cells, viruses create tracks similar to those on 2D surfaces, with trails of cleaved sialic acid reaching several microns in length. Viruses in mucus show a tendency to align their HA-NA axis with their displacement direction, suggesting that protein spatial organization promotes mucus penetration in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C53-C57 demonstrate that the 2D findings extend to a more physiologically relevant 3D mucus environment. The imaging data (Figure 4B-E) shows similar patterns of directional mobility and receptor cleavage. The alignment analysis (C56, Figure 4E) with 2,242 particles provides quantitative support. The inference about in vivo relevance (C57) is appropriately cautious.

result: The morphology of a virus, spatial organization of membrane proteins, and constraints on protein diffusion collectively confer persistent directional mobility that enhances diffusion rate without diminishing adhesion strength.
evaluation: Claims C58-C59 synthesize the major findings of the paper. The conclusion is well-supported by the combination of experimental observations (asymmetric protein distribution, directional mobility, maintained binding) and computational modeling. This represents the central mechanistic insight of the work.

result: Computational simulations predict that directional mobility extends to capsule-shaped particles <200 nm in length, which are produced by filamentous IAV strains. The effect may be suppressed in spherical particles due to lack of a polarization axis and ability to roll on surfaces.
evaluation: Claim C60 is supported by simulation data (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), and C61 is supported by citation to prior literature. However, C62 is speculative reasoning that has not been experimentally tested. The prediction about spherical particles is logical but remains unvalidated. This limits the strength of conclusions about particle shape effects.

result: Mathematical modeling of mucus penetration as a first passage problem predicts that the observed 5-fold increase in diffusion coefficient would proportionally reduce transit time and dramatically increase the fraction of particles reaching the epithelium under high mucociliary clearance rates. Persistent motion is predicted to increase epithelial reach by several orders of magnitude.
evaluation: Claims C63-C65 present mathematical modeling predictions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) based on experimentally measured diffusion coefficients. While the mathematical framework is sound, the model makes simplifying assumptions (1D diffusion, specific parameter values for clearance rates) that may not fully capture in vivo complexity. The predictions are plausible but would require in vivo validation to be considered fully supported.

result: Alternative strategies to accelerate mucus penetration (reducing size, decreasing HA, increasing NA, or uniform NA distribution) would likely reduce binding stability at the cell surface, whereas polarized NA distribution increases diffusion without compromising binding stability.
evaluation: Claim C66 is speculative reasoning about alternative strategies that were not experimentally tested. Claim C67 summarizes the key advantage of the observed mechanism but is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. While the logic is sound and consistent with known HA-NA balance principles, direct experimental comparison of these alternatives would strengthen the conclusion.

result: The fluorescent labeling approach preserves NA enzymatic activity and viruses with labeled HA and NA retain ~85% infectivity, validating the use of labeled viruses for functional studies.
evaluation: Claim C22 is supported by MUNANA assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and C23 by citation to prior work. These methodological validations are important for interpreting all other results, as they demonstrate that the labeling does not fundamentally alter virus function.

result: Background context on IAV infection mechanism, mucosal barriers, virus morphology differences between clinical and laboratory strains, and prior observations of non-uniform HA/NA clustering.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C7-C12 provide established background knowledge supported by citations to prior literature. These contextual claims are well-supported but represent prior work rather than new findings from this study.

result: Prior work showed influenza particles are mobile during sialic acid interactions and that influenza C virus prevents backtracking through receptor destruction. This work shows IAV accomplishes persistent motion through asymmetric distribution of HA and NA activities.
evaluation: Claims C68-C69 accurately cite prior literature, and C70 appropriately positions the current findings in context of previous work. This comparison highlights the novelty of the mechanism discovered in this study.

result: The persistent directional mobility could enhance anomalous diffusion of cylindrical particles in mucus and, analogous to bacterial motility, help explain IAV's ability to penetrate mucus and the prevalence of filamentous morphology in clinical isolates.
evaluation: Claims C71-C73 make speculative connections to prior work on nanoparticle diffusion and bacterial motility. While the analogies are reasonable and the hypothesis about clinical prevalence is plausible, these remain speculative interpretations that would require additional experimental validation, particularly in vivo studies or clinical isolate analysis.

result: The virus strain used is A/WSN/1933 with M1 from A/Udorn/1972, which differs at six residues and confers filamentous morphology, producing particles ranging from sub-diffraction spots to >10 µm in length.
evaluation: Claims C74-C76 describe the experimental system. C75 is supported by citation and C76 by prior work and current observations. These are methodological details that are well-documented.
